# Brewser catalogue — envelope v2

**Status:** contract definition (Phase 1 of the 2026-07 runtime adaptation). No producer emits v2 yet; `scripts/build_catalog.py` still emits v1. The runtime's normalizer (brewser-v8) is built against this spec first; the generator follows per the decided production pipeline at the bottom.

**Machine-readable schema:** [`catalogue.schema.v2.json`](catalogue.schema.v2.json) (Draft-07, same convention as staging's `manifest.schema.json`).
**Fixtures** (`brewser-v8/tests/fixtures/platform/`, regenerated by `brewser-v8/tests/tools/regen_fixtures.py`):

- `catalogue.v1.live.json` — genuine **CI-produced** snapshot of the live v1 catalogue (dated since the 2026-07-25 `publishedAt` backfill; recapture from CI output, never from a local generator run). The v2 example derives from it, so fixture dates and sizes are the production values.
- `catalogue.v1.dateless.json` — the frozen **pre-backfill** snapshot, kept solely as the dateless-tolerance case (`publishedAt` absent → `''`). Must never gain dates. Neither v1 fixture is re-serialized under the pin — they are captures, not producer outputs.
- `catalogue.v2.example.json` — v2 exercising every new field (non-default `source`, `featured`, empty `revoked`).
- `index-fragment.base.example.json`, `index-fragment.ext1.example.json`, `curation.example.json` — producer inputs. Invariant (the generator's golden test): merging the fragments with the curation file per the pipeline below yields `catalogue.v2.example.json` **byte-for-byte**.
- `catalogue.v3-stub.json` (`version: 3`, deliberately hostile below the version field — `"apps": "not-an-array"` — so the guard test proves parse ordering, not coincidence), `catalogue.corrupt.json` (truncated JSON), `catalogue.pre-v1-tiered.json` (the old tiered envelope) — adversarial inputs for the runtime normalizer; not producer outputs, not pinned.
- `stats.example.json` — C2 stats with deliberate gaps: at least one catalogue app absent from stats, and one stats id absent from the catalogue, so the join's failure modes are covered rather than assumed. Not pinned to the golden test.

---

## The envelope

```json
{
  "apps": [
    {
      "categories": ["Apps"],
      "compatibility": ["switch", "web"],
      "developer": "NatureGlass",
      "entry": "index.html",
      "featured": true,
      "genre": ["Music"],
      "id": "com.natureglass.midilab",
      "license": "MIT",
      "logo": "assets/appbanner.jpg",
      "name": "MIDI Lab",
      "permissions": ["Usb"],
      "publishedAt": "2026-06-20T00:00:00Z",
      "sizeBytes": 118944,
      "source": "ext1",
      "summary": "Plain-text summary derived from the manifest description…",
      "version": "2.1.1"
    }
  ],
  "defaultSource": "base",
  "generated": "2026-07-24T12:00:00Z",
  "revoked": [],
  "sources": {
    "base": "https://play.brewser.io",
    "ext1": "https://play1.brewser.io"
  },
  "version": 2
}
```

(Key order is alphabetical at every level — see **Serialization**, which pins it.)

| Field | Type | Required | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `version` | integer | yes | `2` for this shape. **Bumped on every breaking shape change** — this field is the entire compatibility mechanism for arbitrarily-old offline clients. (It was decorative through the v1 era: the envelope changed from tiered to flat while `version` stayed `1`. That must never happen again.) |
| `generated` | string | yes | ISO-8601 UTC timestamp of generation. |
| `sources` | object | yes | Map of source name → **repo root** URL (`https://…`, no `/apps` suffix, no trailing slash). Repo roots, not app roots, so app files *and* artifacts resolve from one table. At least one key. |
| `defaultSource` | string | yes | Must be a key of `sources`. Applied to every entry that omits `source`. |
| `revoked` | array of app ids | yes | Ids the runtime must mark and **block from launch** (see below). Ships as `[]`. |
| `apps` | array | yes | One entry per published app, sorted by `id`. |

## Entry shape

The entry is a **projection** of the app's `manifest.json`, not a verbatim merge. Principle: **carry what's needed to browse and decide; drop what's only needed at launch or after install.** Measured on the live data, the full HTML `description` alone was ~91% of catalogue bytes.

- **Required** (from the manifest, projected): `id`, `name`, `version`, `entry`, `logo`, `categories[]` (≥1), `compatibility[]` (⊆ `switch|web|smartphone|android`, ≥1), `permissions[]`, `developer`, `license`, `publishedAt` (see C1 below).
- **Required** (producer-injected): `summary` (see below), `sizeBytes` (integer — total payload bytes).
- **Optional** (browse filters, from the manifest): `genre[]`, `features[]`, `tags[]`.
- **`source`** (string, optional) — which `sources` key this app's files live under. Omitted ⇒ `defaultSource`. Must be a key of `sources`; an entry naming an unknown source is invalid (the runtime drops it into its parse report, never silently). Stamped at merge time from the fragment that produced the entry — **the fragment is authoritative for location** (see pipeline below); WP's routing decision at intake has no representation in the catalogue.
- **`featured`** (boolean, optional; absent ⇒ false) — operator curation, overlaid at merge time from `curation.json` (WP-exported `_brewser_featured`). **Never sourced from the manifest** — manifests are developer-authored and regenerated on resubmission, which would clobber curation.

**Removed from the catalogue** (still in `manifest.json`, read locally after install): `description` (full HTML), `allowed_origins`, `exitGame`, `fullscreen`, `buttonMapping`, `linked_idea_ids` (verified: nothing in the runtime consumes it at browse time).

Rationale — preserve so this isn't undone later: an app that is *not installed* has no local manifest, so anything absent from the catalogue costs a network round trip per app. Under D2 the user syncs, disconnects, and browses offline for weeks. `permissions` in particular is the **pre-download disclosure** — the user must see what an app wants before committing to it — and `compatibility` is the filter that keeps web-only apps off the Switch.

`id` pattern: `^com\.[a-z0-9]{3,32}\.[a-z0-9]{2,48}$`.
`permissions[]` values are currently Title-Case taxonomy term *names* (`"Usb"`, `"Device Info"`); the runtime normalizes name→slug during the transition. The platform-side move to slugs is a separate track and does not change this envelope.

Unknown fields — envelope-level or entry-level — are **non-breaking**: consumers keep them out of the model but record them in a parse report. Breaking changes (renames, removals, semantic changes) require a `version` bump.

**Last free shape change.** `publishedAt` was added as *required* without a version bump only because no v2 catalogue has ever been published. Once the generator emits v2, adding a required field is a breaking change and costs a `version` bump — this exemption is spent.

## `publishedAt` (C1)

ISO-8601 UTC, in **both** `manifest.json` and the catalogue entry. **Set-once, never re-stamped**: WP rebuilds the manifest on every resubmission *and on every metadata edit*, so a naive build-time stamp would reset the date on every rebuild and pin the app to the top of Most Recent forever — the same clobbering hazard that keeps `featured` out of the manifest.

**The carry-forward set** is the mechanism (DECIDED 2026-07-25): `Brewser_Sub_Manifest::CARRY_FORWARD_FIELDS` names every immutable manifest field in one place; every `build()` call site resolves them via `brewser_sub_resolve_manifest_carry_forward()` — production manifest value **verbatim** → App Post `post_date` (loud log: post-backfill this branch means something upstream is wrong) → now (quiet: the expected branch for a brand-new app). The prior-value read targets the **production** storage repo, never staging (staging app bodies are deleted after promote); a *transient* read failure aborts the rebuild rather than falling through — a fallback on a hiccup is how a set-once field gets silently rewritten. The next immutable field joins the set, not a new one-off.

Semantics (DECIDED 2026-07-25): **first publish = the app's first submission build.** For a brand-new app the stamp happens at build time, before approval — stamping at approval/promote instead would add a fourth manifest-writing flow on the approval path and break promote-copies-verbatim, for a gap that is minutes-to-hours in this solo-approved pipeline. Known, accepted divergence: the WP browse "Most Recent" orders on `post_date` (first approval), so interleaved submit/approve sequences across two apps can order differently on web vs console; operationally negligible today, revisit (stamp-at-first-approval as a single-key patch) only if the pipeline ever becomes multi-tenant. It is *not* `post_modified`, so there is **no `updatedAt`** field. Because `publishedAt` rides the manifest, the fragment producer picks it up from its existing tree walk — no new merge input, `curation.json` stays featured/revoked only — and installed-but-unlisted apps sort correctly in Most Recent from their on-disk manifest.

v1 tolerance: the live v1 catalogue predates the backfill, so v1 entries may lack it — the runtime maps absence to `''` ("no date"), never to an epoch. On v2 entries it is required; a v2 entry without it is dropped into the parse report.

Backfill: the 12 live apps get `publishedAt` from WP (`post_date`); git cannot supply it (history hard-reset 2026-07-21). A content migration in the apps repos, tracked on the WP track.

## `stats.json` (C2)

`downloads` / `ratingAvg` / `ratingCount` change continuously and must **not** enter `catalogue.json` — the catalogue is a pure function of git state, and its diffability is why Option A was chosen. Operational counters live in a separate file at the **base repo root**, served from Pages alongside the catalogue (`https://play.brewser.io/stats.json`), published by **WP-Cron daily** (clients sync weekly at best; fresher is wasted):

```json
{
  "generated": "2026-07-25T03:00:00Z",
  "stats": {
    "com.natureglass.midilab": { "downloads": 412, "ratingAvg": 4.6, "ratingCount": 23 }
  }
}
```

- Keyed by id (a map, not an array — the runtime joins by id). Source: the telemetry aggregates (`swtel_downloads_map()` / `swtel_ratings_list()`) — the same tables the plugin's own Popular and Top Rated sorts are fed from.
- **Publisher presence filter:** WP publishes stats for **catalogue-present ids only** (the id set of the published `catalogue.json`, read before every publish; unreadable catalogue → the run aborts loudly). Telemetry rows for unknown ids — deleted apps, test beacons, typo'd package ids — never reach `stats.json`, and they are excluded **before** the Top Rated corpus is formed (see §Top Rated). Excluded ids are logged; stale rows are purged from the Telemetry admin tab.
- Fetched during sync alongside `catalogue.json`. Joined by id in the platform client; stats ids with no known app are ignored and **recorded** (an app may have been delisted between publications — drift-visibility, not an error). This runtime-side tolerance stays as defense in depth even with the publisher filter above.
- **Not** part of the golden test, **not** covered by the catalogue `version` field, and **not** a function of git state — it is operational data that lives in the repo only because Pages serves from the repo.
- **CI scoping:** the base catalogue workflow must trigger on `apps/**` and `curation.json` only — never on `stats.json` — or every daily stats commit republishes the catalogue.
- Missing, stale, or unparseable `stats.json` is **not** a sync failure: Featured and Most Recent keep working; Popular and Top Rated report themselves unavailable with a reason. Degrade visibly, never silently.
- Machine-readable schema: [`stats.schema.json`](stats.schema.json).

(Alternative considered and rejected: a live WP endpoint — avoids repo commits but couples the sync path to WordPress uptime and adds a third contract surface. Revisit only if daily commits prove genuinely annoying.)

## Top Rated — one rule, computed once, server-side (REVISED 2026-07-25)

**The ranking is computed only by WordPress** and published as `ratingScore` in `stats.json`. Two independent implementations of one rule is the divergence this section exists to prevent, and constants baked into a deployed runtime cannot be tuned: raise the prior weight as the corpus grows and every stale console would rank on the old value forever (D2 skew, unbounded and one-directional).

**The formula (platform-side, normative here):**

```
C = mean of ratingAvg across CATALOGUE-PRESENT apps with ratingCount ≥ 1   (EMPIRICAL corpus mean)
m = BREWSER_RATING_PRIOR_WEIGHT                                            (PHP constant, default 5)
score = (v·R + m·C) / (v + m)                                              rounded to 4 decimals
```

- **The corpus is the catalogue:** rows whose id is not in the published catalogue are excluded *before* `C` is computed (§`stats.json` presence filter) — one stale test row must not shift every score. The conformance-oracle corpus is by definition already post-filter input.

- `C` is the empirical mean, **not a literal**: app ratings skew high, so a fixed midpoint (3.0) compresses every score toward a value no app has, shrinking real differences to noise. On the decision case, empirical `C` gives ~4.77 vs ~4.64 — correct order with the real gap preserved.
- `ratingCount === 0` → **`ratingScore` is omitted entirely** (not 0, not `C`): a Bayesian score with `v = 0` equals the corpus mean, which would rank an unrated app above genuinely mediocre rated ones. Absent means "no data."
- No rated apps → `C` undefined → no scores published.
- `m` is a tunable PHP constant — every client picks up a change on its next sync, which is the entire point of computing server-side.
- The same score drives the WP browse "Top rated" sort (`_brewser_rating_score` meta, hourly cron); `_brewser_rating` stays for display. Console and web must never rank differently.
- **Conformance:** this section is the normative statement. The fixture corpus (`stats.example.json`, generated by `regen_fixtures.py with_rating_scores()`) is a conformance **oracle**: the WP implementation, run over that corpus, must reproduce those exact numbers (formula + edge cases). Its production output will differ — `C` is the empirical mean of whatever corpus it runs over — and that difference is expected, not drift to reconcile.

**Runtime contract:** sort on `ratingScore` descending; ties `publishedAt` desc, then id. An app without `ratingScore` sorts after every scored app; when no app has one, the tab reports unavailable (sparse-data rule). The runtime **never computes a score and has no fallback formula** — a fallback silently ranking on stale constants is worse than an honest gap. `ratingAvg` / `ratingCount` are display fields only ("4.8 ★ (50)"), never ranking inputs.

**Availability floor (console, decided 2026-07-25):** the Top Rated tab is a ranking only when at least **3** library apps carry `ratingScore` (`TOP_RATED_MIN_RATED` in `library-view.ts`); below that it reports unavailable with the count ("Only 1 app rated so far — Top Rated needs 3."). One scored app is a spotlight, two a comparison — neither is a ranking, and with `m = 5` scores barely differentiate below three rated apps anyway. Scores for ids outside the library never count toward the floor. The WP browse "Top rated" **sort** is unaffected — it is a sort order on an always-full list, not a tab that promises a ranking.

This replaces WP's raw-average order, where one 5★ rating outranked fifty ratings averaging 4.8.

## `summary` — source + derivation (deterministic)

**Preferred source (2026-07-27): the human "Short description."** The WP submit form's one-line "Short description" (`post_excerpt`, ≤100 chars) is now emitted into the manifest as `summary` by `Brewser_Sub_Manifest::build()` (only when non-empty), so it flows straight through to the catalogue entry. The runtime shows it under the browse card; the full HTML `description` — **retained in the catalogue** (v1) alongside `summary` — is what the app detail modal renders. When an entry carries no `summary` (a manifest that predates the field, or a blank Short description), the runtime **falls back** to deriving one from the HTML `description` via the algorithm below, so cards never go blank. The fixtures + live v1 capture still exercise the derived path (they have no `summary` yet), which is why the golden test is unaffected.

Derivation (the fallback) is produced from the manifest's HTML `description` (precedent: staging's `index.json` truncates to ≤500). The algorithm is pinned because the golden test is byte-exact:

1. Strip HTML tags (`<[^>]*>` → empty).
2. Decode HTML entities (`&amp;` → `&`, …). Order matters: stripping first means author-written literal `&lt;tag&gt;` text survives as text.
3. Collapse every whitespace run (including `\r\n`) to a single space; trim.
4. If the result is ≤ 400 characters, done.
5. Otherwise cut at the last space at or before character 400 (hard-cut at 399 if there is no space, so the appended ellipsis keeps the result ≤400), `rstrip`, append `…` (U+2026).

Count **characters, not bytes**. Plain text only — no markup reaches the card renderer. Reference implementation: `summarize()` in `regen_fixtures.py`.

## Serialization (pinned — every producer: fragments, `curation.json`, `catalogue.json`)

- UTF-8, no BOM
- `indent=2`
- `ensure_ascii=False` (Python's default emits `—`-style escapes — semantically identical, byte-different)
- `sort_keys=True` (alphabetical at every level)
- LF line endings, single trailing newline

This is not only for the golden test. Option A was chosen partly because the catalogue stays diffable and reviewable in git; unstable key ordering silently destroys that — a regeneration by a different producer would show a whole-file diff with no semantic change. Any Python touching these files passes `encoding='utf-8'` explicitly on every read and write: CI is Linux/UTF-8 and passes regardless — the breakage appears only when a script is run by hand on Windows (default cp1252), which is the worse failure shape.

## URL resolution (the only place URLs are built)

Let `root = sources[app.source ?? defaultSource]`:

- app file → `${root}/apps/${id}/${rel}` (entry: `${root}/apps/${id}/${entry}`; logo: `${root}/apps/${id}/${logo}`)
- artifacts → `${root}/artifacts/${id}.json`
- `versions.json` → global, from the base pin: `https://play.brewser.io/versions.json`

The runtime keeps exactly **one hardcoded URL**: `https://play.brewser.io/catalogue.json` (with `versions.json` alongside). Everything else derives from `sources`. Hosting is GitHub Pages behind CNAMEs — never WordPress, never `raw.githubusercontent.com`; a future hosting move is a DNS change.

## Runtime obligations

**Version guard.** If `version` is greater than the highest version the runtime understands: do **not** overwrite the cached catalogue, keep the last good one, and surface "your Brewser runtime needs updating." A catalogue that fails to parse or validate is likewise never persisted.

**Disk is authoritative for installed apps.** The catalogue only says what is *available*. Absence of an installed app from the catalogue never hides it or blocks it — an interrupted sync, a stale catalogue, and a deliberate delisting are indistinguishable. The one exception:

**`revoked`.** Ids listed here are marked and blocked from launch, even if installed. This is the only catalogue signal allowed to remove local capability, which is why it ships from the first v2 release even though it is always empty today: in a fleet of arbitrarily-old offline clients, the reader must exist before the writer is ever needed. No further revocation machinery exists or should be built now.

**Authority rule.** The catalogue is authoritative for **availability, version, and curation**; the manifest is authoritative for **behaviour** (`entry` resolution at launch, `allowed_origins`, `exitGame`, `fullscreen`, `buttonMapping`, permission enforcement). When the two disagree — normal mid-deploy — that split decides, not read order.

**One-door rule.** If the runtime ever fetches a remote `manifest.json` for a not-installed app (e.g. a future detail view wanting the full description), that fetching and parsing belongs to the platform client. It is a second platform surface, and the same module already parses local manifests. No consumer grows its own manifest fetch.

## v1 compatibility

- v1 flat (`{"version":1, "generated":…, "apps":[…]}` — the current live shape): accepted by the runtime normalizer with implicit `sources = {"base": "https://play.brewser.io"}`, `defaultSource = "base"`, `revoked = []`.
- Pre-v1 tiered (`{"featured":[…], "community":[…], "experimental":[…]}`): **invalid**. Not parsed, not persisted, no migration (nothing is deployed outside the developer's own hardware).

## Production pipeline (DECIDED 2026-07-24 — spec only, nothing implemented yet)

The catalogue stays a **pure function of git state**: `catalogue.json = f(fragments, curation.json)` — reproducible at any commit, diffable, rebuildable after a rebase, and still regenerated on direct repo pushes. WP never composes the catalogue.

**1. Per-repo fragments.** Each repo that holds app files (base and every ext repo), on push to `apps/**`, walks its own `apps/` tree and emits `/index-fragment.json` at the repo root:

```json
{
  "apps": [ { "…": "the catalogue entry projection", "maxFileBytes": 123, "sizeBytes": 456 } ],
  "generated": "<ISO8601Z>",
  "source": "<name>"
}
```

A fragment entry is the **catalogue entry shape minus `source`/`featured`** (stamped/overlaid at merge), **plus `maxFileBytes`**. The fragment producer does the projection: it slims the manifest, derives `summary` (R2 algorithm), and computes `sizeBytes` + `maxFileBytes` from the file walk. Entries sorted by id; serialization pinned.

**`maxFileBytes`** — the largest single file in the app payload. GitHub rejects individual files over 100 MiB at push time (a hard block, not a soft cap), and Unity WebGL builds routinely emit `.data`/`.wasm` files in that range. The fragment producer **fails loudly** when any file exceeds the limit, so the problem surfaces at intake rather than as a confusing CI push error. The **merge strips `maxFileBytes`** — it is a producer/capacity datum, not a browse field. (Capacity context: overall size is governed by the 1 GB-per-site Pages ceiling, not repo size.)

Each repo also continues producing its own `artifacts/<id>.json` (file lists and byte counts come from walking files, so this producer sits with the files under any design). **The fragment is authoritative for app location:** an app is where its fragment says it is.

**Known constraint — manifest byte-stability.** Two manifest serializers exist: the standard intake writes `Brewser_Sub_Manifest::encode()` bytes (pretty, deliberate key order), while the large-intake path sends the manifest through GitHub's `repository_dispatch` payload — which **re-serializes and alphabetizes it** — before the workflow writes it compact-minified. Harmless today (fragments normalize under the serialization pin regardless), but **signed manifests** would need byte-stability that two serializers cannot provide; if catalogue/manifest signing ships (the roadmap `revoked` points at), the large-intake path must first stop round-tripping manifest bytes through the dispatch payload.

**2. WP curation export.** WP writes `curation.json` to the **base** repo root via the existing `repository_dispatch` machinery, on approve / feature-toggle / revoke:

```json
{ "featured": ["<id>"], "generated": "<ISO8601Z>", "revoked": ["<id>"] }
```

No location data — curation carries only `featured` and `revoked`.

**3. Base-CI merge.** The base repo's CI holds the source list (name → repo root URL, i.e. the envelope's `sources` table) and builds `catalogue.json`: fetch each fragment over its Pages URL, concatenate `apps`, strip `maxFileBytes`, stamp each non-default entry with its fragment's `source` (base entries omit it ⇒ `defaultSource`), overlay `featured` from curation, copy `revoked` to the top level, emit the v2 envelope sorted by id with `CATALOG_VERSION = 2`, pinned serialization. Adding an `ext2` later is one line in the source list. Reference implementation: `merge()` in `brewser-v8/tests/tools/regen_fixtures.py`.

**4. Fail loudly — never emit a partial catalogue.** A catalogue that silently omits an app is indistinguishable from a delisting, the exact ambiguity D2a exists to remove. Build failures:

- any fragment unfetchable or unparseable
- the same id present in two fragments (ambiguous location)
- a `featured` id with no fragment entry

Explicitly **not** a failure: a `revoked` id with no fragment entry — revocation may mean the files were deleted, so revoked ids are exempt from the presence check.

**Merge-level validation** (in addition to the schema): `defaultSource` ∈ `sources`; every stamped `source` ∈ `sources`; entries sorted by id; folder name == manifest `id`; required manifest fields present. Draft-07 cannot express the cross-field rules — they are producer code + runtime normalizer checks.

**Golden test:** merging the two example fragments with the example curation file must reproduce `catalogue.v2.example.json` byte-for-byte (fixtures listed at the top).

## Cross-schema consistency (R5)

Every field the catalogue entry **requires** must be guaranteed present by staging's `manifest.schema.json`, or be producer-injected — otherwise a valid submission breaks the catalogue build with a legitimate input. Current mapping (staging schema requires 14 fields):

| Catalogue-required | Guaranteed by |
|---|---|
| `id`, `name`, `version`, `entry`, `logo`, `categories`, `compatibility`, `permissions`, `developer`, `license` | manifest schema `required` |
| `publishedAt` | manifest schema `required` (added 2026-07-25; WP builder must emit it set-once — until the WP change lands, staging CI rejects new submissions, which is the intended forcing function) |
| `summary` | fragment producer, derived from `description` — **manifest-required**, so the input always exists |
| `sizeBytes` | fragment producer (file walk) |
| `source`, `featured` (optional) | merge (fragment identity / curation) |

Manifest-required fields *not* projected into the catalogue — `description`, `allowed_origins`, `exitGame`, `fullscreen` — are launch-time, manifest-authoritative (see the authority rule). **No gap exists today.** Standing rule: any future addition to the catalogue-required list must name its guarantor (manifest schema `required` or a producer) in this table, in the same change.

## Remaining WP-track items (separate track — not this task)

- `curation.json` publisher (dispatch on approve / feature-toggle / revoke)
- D5 permission slugs in the manifest builder
- ext-repo CI workflow (fragment + artifacts)
- `POST /rate` (brewser-auth): validate `packageId` against existing apps before the upsert — deferred from the C-track close-out (Phase 5); the presence filter keeps orphans out of `stats.json`, this closes the intake side so stale test rows stop accumulating at the source

Done 2026-07-25 (kept for the record): `publishedAt` set-once carry-forward in `Brewser_Sub_Manifest::build()` + live backfill of the 12 apps (B2/B3); `stats.json` daily WP-Cron publisher with the presence filter (C2); Top Rated ranking rule fixed both places — shared `Brewser_Sub_Rating_Score`, server-published `ratingScore` (C1).
